2358.t: From κλεπ- (klep-, present stem of κλέπτω (kléptō, “to steal”)) + -της (-tēs, masculine agentive suffix).

2313.t: From Ἀντίοχος (Ăntĭ́okhos, “Antiochus, name of several Seleucid kings”) + -εια (-eiă).

2302.t: Corresponding noun of Ancient Greek ἀγείρω (ăgeírō, “to gather”), with later senses from ἄγω (ắgō, “to lead”) (though Beekes considers all senses to derive only from ἄγω (ắgō)).

2345.t: PIE word *dwís Nominal formation from διαιτάω (dĭaitắō, “to treat, handle”).

2346.t: According to Beekes, probably from Pre-Greek, based on an analysis δίπ-σα (díp-sa) lacking clear semantic and morphological correspondences in other Indo-European branches, as well as the existence of variants with φ and β.

2380.t: From Proto-Hellenic *stéřřa, from Proto-Indo-European *stérih₂. By surface analysis, στεῖρος (steîros) + -α (-ă).

2363.t: The connection with κίνδαξ (kíndax, “quick, nimble”), ὀνοκίνδιος (onokíndios, “donkey-driver”) is formally attractive.

2361.t: Traditionally derived from a reduplicated form of Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, turn”).

2372.t: Derived from Proto-Indo-European *p(y)eh₂w- (“to hit, strike”). Cognates include Latin paviō.

2362.t: Probably from the same Pre-Greek root of κηφήν (kēphḗn, “drone”).

2324.t: εἷς (heîs, “one”, masculine and neuter stem: ἑν-) + δέκα (dékă, “ten”)

2388.t: From a West Semitic language such as Hebrew סַפִּיר (sappîr); originally from Assyrian Akkadian šipirtu (“lapis lazuli”).

2339.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *glewbʰ- Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *glúbʰeti Proto-Hellenic *glúpʰō Ancient Greek γλύφω From Proto-Hellenic *glúpʰō, from Proto-Indo-European *glewbʰ- (“to split, carve”).

2387.t: From συν- (sun-, “with”) + the root of μάχη (mákhē, “battle”).

2333.t: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָאֵל (mīḵāʾēl, “Michael”, literally “Who is like God?”).

2366.t: From μή (mḗ, “not”) + ἔτι (éti, “yet”), with κ (k) by analogy with οὐκέτι (oukéti).

2399.t: Seemingly, a formation with the suffix -λός (-lós) like στρεβλός (streblós) and τυφλός (tuphlós), but without obvious etymology.

2368.t: Some have proposed a Proto-Indo-European *mand- (“enclosure”), cognate with Sanskrit मन्दुरा (mandurā, “stable; bed”) and possibly related to μανδάκης (mandákēs, “band to tie trusses”), μάνδαλος (mándalos, “bolt”), and Proto-West Germanic *mandu…

2398.t: From the root of χράομαι (khráomai, “to use, desire”) + -ιμος (-imos, “-able, -like”).

2338.t: Considered Pre-Greek, but also Semitic, relating to Hebrew בֹּסֶר (boser, “unripe grape”), Arabic بُسْر (busr, “unripe dates”), Jewish Babylonian Aramaic בֻּסְרָא (busrā), בּוּסְרָא (busrā, “unripe grape”), Classical Syriac ܒܣܪܐ (*busrā, “unripe grape”).

2309.t: From ἀπο- (ăpo-, “from, back”) + αἰτέω (aitéō, “to ask, beg”).

2394.t: From φάρμακον (phármakon, “herb, drug”). The noun only in biblical Greek, for φαρμακεύς (pharmakeús).

2343.t: From δικάζω (dĭkắzō, “to judge”) + -της (-tēs, “-er”, masculine agent-noun suffix): Literally, “judger”.

2322.t: Beekes points out the absence of cognates in other Indo-European languages and considers the word to be of Pre-Greek origin.

2390.t: Beekes notes comparisons by Bezzenberger and Fick to Proto-Germanic *þakjaną (“to burn”), which he notes is isolated within Germanic, and takes the Greek, per Furnee, from a Pre-Greek substrate.

2389.t: From the Septuagint rendition of Hebrew שֵׁכָר (šēḵār), used to refer to strong drinks, from Proto-Semitic *šikar- (“alcoholic drink”).

2370.t: Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to bind”) or a loan from an Indo-Iranian source.

2382.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱe? Proto-Indo-European *ḱómder.? Proto-Indo-European *sem-der.? Proto-Hellenic *ksún Ancient Greek σύν (sún) Ancient Greek συν- (sun-) Proto-Indo-European *(s)kep-? Proto-Hellenic *kopt͏̌ō Ancient Greek κόπτω (kóptō)…

2397.t: From χόρτος (khórtos, “fodder”) + -άζω (-ázō, suffix to form a verb).

2381.t: From συν- (sŭn-, “with; together”) + καλέω (kăléō, “to call”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁-.

2349.t: From ζυγόν (zŭgón, “the yoke of a plow or carriage; a crossbar of the lyre”) + -όω (-óō, “verbal suffix”).

2329.t: From ὁρμή (hormḗ, “start, impetus, rush, attack, effort”) + -άω (-áō, “verbal suffix”).

2321.t: According to Beekes, a denominative from *ἐρεϝ-(ε)ν- (*erew-(e)n-), a noun itself derived from earlier *ἐρεϝω (*erewō), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rew-.
